passage:
Thursday, late.
For a week Farid, my husband, has been tilting his phone away when he texts, smiling at it sometimes. Last night my stomach twisted. At lunch today Sabina said, "Just check his phone while he sleeps. Everyone does."
I didn't. I thought about how I'd feel if he read my chats with my sister, all the silly stuff and the complaints about his mother. Those are mine. They aren't a betrayal.
So after dinner I just said, "You've been smiling at your phone a lot. Anything I should know?" He laughed and went a bit pink. "It's the school group. We're planning a reunion, and they're teasing me about my old haircut." He offered to show me. I said no; I believed him.
If something affects us, I expect him to tell me. The rest can be his.
Jyoti

qa.q: What did Sabina suggest at lunch?
qa.a: Sabina said, "Just check his phone while he sleeps."

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling last night, and what changed Jyoti's mind?
qa.a: Jyoti's stomach twisted with suspicion, but imagining Farid reading the chats with Jyoti's sister made it clear that private messages aren't betrayal.

qa.q: Which choice by Jyoti protected trust, and why?
qa.a: Jyoti asked Farid directly instead of checking his phone, which respected his privacy while still inviting honesty about anything that affects them.

qa.q: How might Farid feel when Jyoti asks instead of checking his phone?
qa.a: He probably feels trusted and a little embarrassed, which is why he laughed, went pink and offered to show the phone.

grounding: An adult notices a partner's private texting, resists the urge to check the phone, and trusts his inner life while still expecting honesty about what affects them.

Ten minutes before the inter-school music round, with the hall already filling, Bhavna grabbed her friend Rekha's arm backstage. "Tell me honestly. Am I okay?"
Rekha prided herself on never sugar-coating. "Honestly? You go flat on the high notes. You'll probably embarrass yourself." She said it quickly, almost pleased with how clear it sounded.
There was no time to practise, nothing Bhavna could fix. Her face went pale. On stage she started too quietly and never recovered.
Afterwards Rekha told the others, "Someone had to be real with her." But on the bus home she remembered the small satisfied feeling she'd had while saying it, and it didn't feel like honesty any more. It felt more like winning.

qa.q: When did Bhavna ask Rekha for an honest opinion?
qa.a: Ten minutes before the inter-school music round, backstage.

qa.q: What did Rekha realise on the bus home?
qa.a: She realised her comment had come with a small satisfied feeling, so it felt more like winning than honesty.

qa.q: What could Rekha have said ten minutes before the round?
qa.a: With no time to fix anything, she could have offered encouragement, like reminding Bhavna to breathe, and saved honest notes for later when they could help.

qa.q: How did Rekha's words affect Bhavna on stage?
qa.a: They shook her confidence; she went pale, started too quietly and never recovered.

People ask why Pranav still trusts my opinion. It's because of the ice-cream cart. We were twenty, and he wanted to put all his savings into a cart outside our college. I thought it was a bad plan: the college shuts for two months in the rains.
My first instinct was to say it at his birthday dinner, in front of everyone, with a joke. I didn't. My second instinct was to say nothing and let him find out. I didn't do that either.
I waited till the next morning, just us, and said, "I love that you want to build something. Can I tell you the one thing that worries me?" Then I asked about the monsoon months. He went quiet, then said, "Sangeeta, you're right," and pulled out a notebook. He opened a tea stall with a roof instead.

The rain had knocked out the streetlights, so Sahil and Ganga stood under the bus-stop roof in the dark, waiting for a bus already twenty minutes late.
"Can I say something that's been bothering me?" Ganga said. "I've been trying to find the right way for a week." She took a breath. "At the studio, you keep interrupting the junior designers. They've stopped speaking in meetings. I don't think you see it."
Sahil's face went hot. He wanted to say she was exaggerating. But he noticed her hands twisting the strap of her bag, and how carefully she had chosen each word.
The bus finally splashed up. On the ride he replayed Tuesday's meeting and the junior who had started a sentence and stopped. "Thanks," he texted her that night. "That can't have been easy to say."

qa.a: He felt stung and defensive, his face hot, but noticing her twisting hands and careful words showed him she cared, so he listened.

qa.a: He replayed Tuesday's meeting, remembered the junior who stopped mid-sentence, and texted Ganga to thank her.

On their evening walk round the colony park in Hyderabad, Shalini slowed down near the swings. "Pradeep, I'm only saying this because I've known you since school." He laughed. "Uh oh."
"You've borrowed from three of us this year and paid everyone back late. Nobody says anything. But they've stopped inviting you to plan trips, and I think that's why."
Pradeep stopped walking. His ears burned. He wanted to list every reason: the rent, his mother's bills. Instead he stared at the swings. She hadn't said it in the group or by text. She had waited for a quiet walk and said it looking at him.
"That stings," he said finally.
"I know. I'd rather it stung from me."
Two days later he messaged her a list of what he owed, with dates. "Hold me to it?"

Parenting notebook, 3 March.
Nitin (5) knocked the clay pot off the balcony ledge while racing his car. I heard the crash. "Who did this?" nearly came out. I stopped, because that question would only get me "Not me."
Instead I said, "The pot fell. Are you okay?" He nodded, eyes huge. Then he whispered, "My car hit it."
I told him, "Thank you for telling me. The truth matters more to me than any pot." We swept up together. He kept checking my face, but by bedtime he was choosing a plant for a new pot.
Ayesha

qa.a: That question would only invite "Not me", so Ayesha described what happened and checked he was okay, making the truth easy to say.

qa.a: He would likely feel safer confessing, since the truth brought thanks and calm repair rather than anger.
